column2: The title of the observed scientific literature.

column5: The URL link to the observed scientific literature.
column6: The unique numerical identifier that is assigned to books and book-like products published internationally.
column7: The scientific journal the literature was published in.
column8: If published in a scientific journal, this is the volume that the paper was published in.
column9: If published in a scientific journal, this is the page of the volume that this paper is in. If given a range, list the first page in the range.
column10: The first author of the literature.
column12: The date that the literature was published. (mm-dd-yyyy)
column13: The most recent version of the observed scientific literature.
column14: The unique researcher IDs of any contributors to the data in the literature.
column15: Licensing terms of the observed scientific literature. (MIT; open access or subscribe)
column16: The raw text from an "Experimental" section of the literature.
column17: The title of the literature the peak is observed in.
column18: The page number (of the pdf) of the literature that the table is located on.
column19: The title of the table the peak data is displayed in.
column20: The description of the table given in the observed literature.
column21: A list of references specified in the table or in context of the table. (Usually presented as [130-132, 134-136] or a similar format and may require further interpretation)
column22: A description of the instruments used in the spectral data measurements (spectrometer, laser, detector, etc.).
column23: The resolution of the spectrometer used (4 cm^-1, etc.).
column24: The units used for the resolution of the spectrometer used (cm^-1).
column25: The wavelength of the laser used to capture the observed spectroscopy data.
column26: The power of the laser used to capture the observed spectroscopy data (measured in mW). If a pulsed laser was used, this is the average power delivered over the course of the laser pulses.
column27: The spot size diameter of the laser used during measurement (2 micrometers, etc.)
column28: The duration of laser pulses (Continuous if not pulsed)
column29: The duration that the detector collected photons from the analyte.
column30: A description of the objective lens used for the experiment.
column31: The upper bound of the spectral range observed from the experiment in cm^-1.
column32: The lower bound of the spectral range observed in the experiment. in cm^-1
column33: The strategy used to capture the data from the detector (static, average, time-series, etc.)
column34: The temperature of the analyte during the measurement.
column35: The unit of temperature of the analyte during the measurement (C, F, K).
column36: The type of spectroscopy technique used to measure the peaks (Raman, IR, SERS).
column37: The specific substance or chemical constituent that is being measured. This is the "target" of the measurement.
column38: The high-level category describing the fundamental nature of the analyte as a physical or biological entity. (Polymer, Tissue, Environmental Sample, Biomolecule, etc.) (Qualitatively describes form, not chemistry)
column39: The structural or functional chemical family to which the analyte belongs, based on IUPAC nomenclature. (Alcohol, Ketone, Ester, Alkaloid, etc.) (Describes chemistry)
column40: The role that this analyte plays in the measurement (target, reference, internal_standard, matrix_component, impurity, dopant, substrate_modifier)
column41: The plain text string that identifies the observed chemical compound by the SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) standard.
column42: The string of numbers, separated by hyphens that identify the observed chemical compound (as labeled in the CAS registry).
column43: The name of the chemical compound used as a solvent in the experiment.
column44: A list of any other chemicals/substances in the sample that are not being targeted for observation (qualitative description).
column45: The quantitative ratio of the amount of analyte relative to its sample.
column46: The raw text used to describe the concentration of the analyzed solution. (This is usually found in the experimental section or the results section)
column47: The phase of the analyte that it is observed in (solid crystal, powder, solution, vapor, etc.)
column48: The phase of the solvent that the analyte is observed in (solid, liquid, vapor, etc.)
column49: The qualitative description of the procedures taken to prepare the spectroscopic measurement of the analyte.
column50: The unit of the reported shift (usually in cm^-1).
column51: The upper bound of the range for the peak.
column52: The lower bound of the range for the peak.
column53: The single value of the peak (if only one is given).
column54: The width of the peak measured at half the peak height, where intensity is half of the maximum intensity of the peak. (FWHM "Full Width at Half Maximum")(usually in cm^-1)
column55: Additional details about the peak assignment from the literature. Include relative intensity strength as documented by the author of the literature (vs, s, m, w, vw, etc.) and polarization details (p, dp, etc.) with keys to specify if necessary. Also include any baseline correction if stated in literature.
column56: The specific integer assigned to the vibration (4, 10, 3b).
column57: The notation convention used to assign the mode index (Mulliken, Herzberg, Wilson Numbering, Wilson-Decius-Cross, or descriptive)
column58: The shorthand identifier used to assign the vibrational mode in literature (v4, v10, etc.). This follows specific naming conventions (Mulliken, Herzberg, Wilson Numbering, Wilson-Decius-Cross, or descriptive).
column59: The geometry of the structural environment (linear, bent, trigonal planar, trigonal pyramidal, tetrahedral, square planar, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral, etc.)
column60: The machine-readable plain text label for the point group of the structural environment (A1g, C2v, D3h, Td, etc.). ([getzenquery.com](https://www.getzenquery.com/tools/molecular-symmetry-analyzer/))
column61: The symmetry label given to the vibrational mode using the Mulliken labeling convention. (A', a'', B, b, T, t, e, E, g-sub, u-sub)
column62: The descriptive label of the vibrational symmetry (symmetric, antisymmetric, degenerate, etc.).
column63: The descriptive label of the vibrational motion (stretch, bend, twist, rock etc.)
column64: The irreducible label of the vibrational symmetry in machine-readable, plain text, following the Mulliken notation convention (A1g, B2u, E_prime, A1g_sym, etc.)
column65: The descriptive label of the vibrational geometry (in-plane, out-of-plane, radial, tangential, etc.).
column66: The descriptive label of the vibrational phase (in-phase, out-of-phase, etc.).
column67: The distinct, identifiable bond in the molecule that is analyzed in the table (C—C, N=C=N, etc.) (Use SMILES format).
column68: The raw text that is used to report the vibrational mode assignment, if applicable (sym. str., C—C skel. def., etc.) (raw text. non-standardized).
column69: The confidence assigned to a vibrational mode as stated in the literature if applicable. Provide proper context (0.7 out of a 1.0 scale / "certain" vs. "probable").
column70: The specific arrangement of atoms that behaves predictably in spectra (these are substructures that produce characteristic spectral peaks) (Raw qualitative data descriptions, be aware of controlled vocabulary).
column71: The specific bond within the analyte that is being targeted for peak assignment. (Raw data, non-standardized)
column72: Raw descriptive text to describe where a group sits within a molecule. (terminal, internal, axial, endocyclic, exocyclic, backbone)
column73: The base material of the substrate used in the measurement (Ag, Au, Cu, Au–Ag alloy, Si + Au coating, etc.) (Follows naming conventions defined by IUPAC).
column74: The described structure (and any supporting structure) of the substrate (raw text)("Ag nanograss SERS substrate", "silver nanorod array substrates", "Au NPs on a regularly arranged ZrO2 nanoporous structure", etc.) (can be expressed with abbreviations like ns, nr, nf, etc. which may require a key)
column75: The manufacturing process of the substrate as described in the literature. (Raw paragraph description from literature)(ISO/TS 80004-8 is a resource for nanomanufacturing vocabulary.)
column76: The raw text description of how the substrate was prepared for the experiment (Ex: "BCP vapors were sprayed onto a CsI substrate maintained at approximately -190 C by boiling nitrogen.")
column77: The area of the region of the substrate exposed to the analyte and laser (4mm^2, etc.)
column78: The reported dimensions of the substrate used in the measurement (1 x 1cm, region diameter of 2mm, etc.)
column79: A complete description of the substrate used in the SERS experiment. (Raw descriptive text extracted from literature. Ex: "In this study, a SERS-active substrate with Au NPs on a regularly arranged ZrO2 nanoporous structure was utilized to obtain the SERS spectrum of inpatient samples from COVID-19 patients.")
column80: A description of the preprocessing methods used.

column2: The infrared and Raman spectra of the pentafluorodhyl halides
column16: Pentafluoroethyl chloride was made available through the courtesy of Professor J. J. Martin of the Chemical Engineering Department of the University of Michigan, who had obtained it from the Jackson laboratories of the E. I. DuPont de Nemours Co. It had been prepared for PVT studies and was further purified by trap to trap distillation. Pentafluoroethyl bromide and iodide were synthesized in this laboratory by the procedure of VON GROSSE et al. [4]. Perfluoropropionic acid, kindly supplied by the Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Co., was neutralized by Ag2O, and the silver salt decarboxylated by reaction with the appropriate halogen. The product was purified by passage over KOH and P2O5 and was further purified before use by several trap to trap fractionations in a vacuum line. A constant vapor pressure was taken as an indication of purity. The observed spectra show no indication of the presense of sizeable quantities of impurities. The infrared spectra were recorded by a Perkin-Elmer Model 21 double beam spectrometer equipped with both CaF2, and NaCl prisms. The Raman spectra were recorded photographically by a Gaertner two prism spectrograph with a linear dispersion of 16 A/mm. Details of the Raman spectrographic apparatus have been published previously [5]. The Raman spectra of the liquid pentafluoroethyl halides were determined at about -40C, while the spectra of the gases were determined at room temperature and a pressure of about 5 atm. The depolarization ratios of the liquids were determined by the two exposure method using Polaroid cylinders around the sample tubes to polarize the incident light. C2F5I showed photochemical decomposition even at low temperatures, liberating free iodine, and therefore it was not possible to determine the Raman spectrum of gaseous C2F5I. The infrared spectra of the compounds are reproduced in Fig. 1 and microphotometer records of the Raman spectra are reproduced in Figs. 2 and 3.

Martin of the Chemical Engineering Department of the University of Michigan, who had obtained it from the Jackson laboratories of the E. I. DuPont de Nemours Co. It had been prepared for PVT studies and was further purified by trap to trap distillation. Pentafluoroethyl bromide and iodide were synthesized in this laboratory by the procedure of VON GROSSE et al. [4]. Perfluoropropionic acid, kindly supplied by the Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Co., was neutralized by Ag2O, and the silver salt decarboxylated by reaction with the appropriate halogen. The product was purified by passage over KOH and P2O5 and was further purified before use by several trap to trap fractionations in a vacuum line. A constant vapor pressure was taken as an indication of purity. The observed spectra show no indication of the presense of sizeable quantities of impurities. The infrared spectra were recorded by a Perkin-Elmer Model 21 double beam spectrometer equipped with both CaF2, and NaCl prisms. The Raman spectra were recorded photographically by a Gaertner two prism spectrograph with a linear dispersion of 16 A/mm. Details of the Raman spectrographic apparatus have been published previously [5]. The Raman spectra of the liquid pentafluoroethyl halides were determined at about -40C, while the spectra of the gases were determined at room temperature and a pressure of about 5 atm. The depolarization ratios of the liquids were determined by the two exposure method using Polaroid cylinders around the sample tubes to polarize the incident light. C2F5I showed photochemical decomposition even at low temperatures, liberating free iodine, and therefore it was not possible to determine the Raman spectrum of gaseous C2F5I. The infrared spectra of the compounds are reproduced in Fig. 1 and microphotometer records of the Raman spectra are reproduced in Figs. 2 and 3.

column2: The Infrared and Raman Spectra of CF3OF
column16: The sample of CF30F was prepared in this laboratory. Carbon monoxide and fluorine at atmospheric pressure were passed simultaneously over silver fluoride to form F2CO. The F2CO was then further fluorinated in the presence of AgF2 to form the CF30F. Various flow rates were tried. The method is not the same as that described by Kellogg and Cady, the only others to report the preparation of CF3OF, but they do mention this procedure. CF4, F2CO, and HF were present as impurities, as could be noted from the spectrum. F2CO was present to the extent of about 5 inches Hg per atmosphere pressure of the sample studied. A good knowledge of the spectra of these impurities exists, so that for the most part it was possible to eliminate bands due to them from the spectra. The infrared absorption spectrum of CF3OF in the gas state was investigated over the range from 2 to 25mu by means of two Perkin-Elmer prism spectrometers. A double-beam Model 21 was used for the NaCI region. The region from 15-25mu was studied with a Model 12-C using a KBr prism. The entire spectrum was recorded at a pressure of 24 inches Hg, and regions of strong and weak absorption at lower and higher pressures, respectively. The cell length was 10 cm. When using NaCI and KBr windows on the cell, there was noted the formation of "window bands," mostly in the region 2-1Omu, presumably due to the reaction of the gas with the window material. This absorption persisted when the cell was evacuated. It was possible, nevertheless, to observe in these regions by using CaF 2 windows. Also, the presence of such bands could be determined by noting that they remained constant in intensity (allowing time for them to form) as the gas pressure was varied. The Raman spectrum of the liquid was photographed by means of a Lane-Wells spectrograph. The standard Lane-Wells mercury arc excitation unit was used. Appropriate filters were used to eliminate the background and excitation from mercury lines other than from the desired parent line. The Raman shift at 250 cm-1 was found using 5460A as the parent; all others were found as shifts from 4358A. The liquid sample, which boils at about minus 94°C, was contained in a glass Raman tube about one-half inch in diameter inserted in a Dewar. The Dewar was equipped with a plane window to permit exit of the Raman light and was so made that liquid filters could be poured in to surround the sample. The sample was maintained in the liquid state by a stream of cold, dried nitrogen that had passed through coils placed in liquid nitrogen. The Raman spectrum was recorded on Eastman Tri-X Panchromatic film. A slit width of 150 microns was used with exposures varied from ~ to 3 hours. No polarization data were secured.

column2: Vibrational Spectra of Pentachlorocyclopropane
column16: The sample of PCCP was provided by Professor Robert West of the University of Wisconsin. Since NMR and gas-phase chromatography showed the sample to be at least 99% pure, it was used without further purification.The PCCP sample was stored in an evacuated tube at 5 degrees C. Except for transferring the liquid-phase samples into the infrared cell, all sample handling procedures were carried out under vacuum. A Spex Ramalog DUV spectrometer equipped witha Spectra-Physics Model 171 Ar+ laser was used to record the Raman spectrum of liquid PCCP. A powerof approximately 100 mW was used at 514.5 nm, with the sample sealed in a glass capillary. Raman spectra of strong sharp lines should be accurate to +-2 cm-1.Infrared spectra of PCCP vapor were recorded usinga Nicolet 7199 Fourier transform interferometer equipped with a KBr/Ge beam splitter and a liquid nitrogen-cooled MCT detector. The gaseous sample was housed at its ambient vapor pressure in a 15 cm O-ring cell fitted with KBr windows. Liquid- and solid-phase IR spectra of PCCP were obtained with a Perkin-ElmerModel 621 spectrophotometer. A KBr cell of approximately 0.025 mm spacing was used for the liquid-phase spectrum, and the solid phase spectrum was collected by condensing PCCP vapor on to a liquid nitrogen-cooled CsI substrate (ca- 190 " C ) held in a typical infrared cold cell having CsI windows. The polycrystal-line solid was repeatedly annealed until no further spectral changes were observed. Condensed-phase IR frequencies should be accurate to +-2 cm-1 and the FTIR gas-phase frequencies should be accurate to better than 1 cm-1.

Since NMR and gas-phase chromatography showed the sample to be at least 99% pure, it was used without further purification.The PCCP sample was stored in an evacuated tube at 5 degrees C. Except for transferring the liquid-phase samples into the infrared cell, all sample handling procedures were carried out under vacuum. A Spex Ramalog DUV spectrometer equipped witha Spectra-Physics Model 171 Ar+ laser was used to record the Raman spectrum of liquid PCCP. A powerof approximately 100 mW was used at 514.5 nm, with the sample sealed in a glass capillary. Raman spectra of strong sharp lines should be accurate to +-2 cm-1.Infrared spectra of PCCP vapor were recorded usinga Nicolet 7199 Fourier transform interferometer equipped with a KBr/Ge beam splitter and a liquid nitrogen-cooled MCT detector. The gaseous sample was housed at its ambient vapor pressure in a 15 cm O-ring cell fitted with KBr windows. Liquid- and solid-phase IR spectra of PCCP were obtained with a Perkin-ElmerModel 621 spectrophotometer. A KBr cell of approximately 0.025 mm spacing was used for the liquid-phase spectrum, and the solid phase spectrum was collected by condensing PCCP vapor on to a liquid nitrogen-cooled CsI substrate (ca- 190 " C ) held in a typical infrared cold cell having CsI windows. The polycrystal-line solid was repeatedly annealed until no further spectral changes were observed. Condensed-phase IR frequencies should be accurate to +-2 cm-1 and the FTIR gas-phase frequencies should be accurate to better than 1 cm-1.

The alcohol was converted to the ester of p-toluenesulfonic acid by treatment with the acid chloride and pyridine and then hydrolyzed with cold H2SO4 . The ester was converted into the desired halide by treatment with the appropriate alkali halide in beta, beta-primedihydroxyethyl ether (2). Samples were purified by distillation. The sample of CF3CH2Br was supplied by Dr. J. S. Lan of E. I. du I’ont de Nemours and Company.  B. INSTRAMENTATION The infrared spectra were obtained with a Perkin-Elmer Model 21 double  beam recording spectrophotometer over the range of 2 to 24 microns, using  interchangeable CaF2 , NaCl, and KBr optics. For gas spectra, 10-cm Pyrex  cells with NaCl or KBr windows were used. Sealed cells of thickness 0.025 to 0.1mm aud capillary films between KBr plates were used to obtain the spectrum of liquid CF3CH2I. Gaseous CF3CH2I was also observed from 25 to 34 microns in a 10-cm cell with KRS-5 windows using a spectrometer built around a Perkin-Elmer Model 99 double-pass monochromator with a CsBr prism. The Raman equipment used was an Applied Research Laboratories spectrograph with a Schmidt-type camera of about f/2.5 aperture and a dispersion of 15A mm near 4358A. Eastman Kodak XXX panchromatic and DuPont High Speed panchromatic No. 428 sheet films were used and were developed for 7 min in Eastman Kodak DK-60a. Exposure times varied from 1 to 72 hours depending on the caompounds studied. Polarization measurements were made by placing cylinders of “Polaroid” sheet with the polarization parallel and perpendicular in turn around the sample tube during the longer exposures. The exciting source was a Toronto-type mercury arc. The CF3CH2Br sample, bp 26.4C, was cooled by circulating air through an ice salt bath and then through a glass cryostat surrounding the sample tube. Since CF3CH2F boils at -24.7C, it was necessary to circulatr air cooled by passing through a dry ice-trichloroethylene bath. CF3C H2I samples, bp about 55C, were kept sufficiently cool by circulating a solution of Rhodamine 5 GDN extra which acted as a filter to reduce background near the 4358A exciting line.
